title: Love, and do what you will
hook: Augustine's line: love, then do what you want, because love will guide it

segments.voice: Yesterday was the block close on prayer: many doors, one house. Your line was one way, kept. Which way did you choose to keep this month? Today a new block opens: living it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

"Love, and do what thou wilt." That's a bishop talking. Augustine is preaching through the first letter of John, a short letter that keeps circling back to one word, and in the middle of a sermon he folds the whole moral life into one short command. Do what you want? From a bishop? It sounds like a permission slip, and it can be quoted like one: to excuse a shortcut, a betrayal, a cruelty that felt honest at the time. Today a new block begins on the path: living it, Christian ethics. It opens with Augustine's line, because in its place it means something much harder than it sounds.

Look at what Augustine is talking about when he says it. Not doing whatever feels good. He's talking about correction. In the same sermon he sets two scenes side by side. A father disciplines his son, and it looks harsh. A kidnapper is gentle with a child he has stolen, and it looks kind. Which one loves? You can't tell from the outside. You have to look at the root. That's his point: the same act can grow from love or from something else entirely. Then comes the line, and right after it, the examples. If you keep silent, keep silent out of love. If you speak up, speak up out of love. If you correct, correct out of love. If you spare, spare out of love. Augustine isn't inventing this. He's reading the letter in front of him: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God." And Paul, writing to Rome, lists the commandments, do not kill, do not steal, and says they're all summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself: "love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." So the rules aren't thrown out. They're gathered up. That's why this block starts here. Over the coming days the path walks through the commandments one at a time, and Augustine's line is the lens: each rule is what love looks like in one corner of life. In his sermon, love isn't a warm mood. It wants the other person's real good, even when that costs you their approval. That makes it a stricter test than any rule, not a looser one.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one choice against love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one decision waiting for you today: a reply you owe, a no you're dreading, a correction you might give, a kindness you might skip. Hold it up and ask Augustine's question. What's at the root here? Love for this person? Or fear, or pride, or wanting to be liked? Don't decide yet. Just look at the root, honestly, for as long as the bell allows. If you pray, you can hold the choice before God in silence. The bell holds the time.
Love. In Augustine's line, the root every act should grow from: wanting the other person's real good, whether that means speaking up or staying quiet.
Your line: love decides. Today, when that choice comes, let the root decide it, even if the act turns out stricter, or gentler, than you expected. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Some Christian teachers quote Augustine's "love, and do what you will" when teaching that love of God and neighbor is the heart of the moral life, and some preachers pair it with Paul's words that love is the fulfilling of the law.

fork.setup: you're a parent. your child is about to do something that will hurt them, and saying no will make them furious with you. Augustine's line is love, and do what you will. what does it ask of you?
options: say yes: love means keeping them happy.
say no, out of love, and take the anger.
say nothing: it isn't your business.
fork.reveal: Augustine's own example is a father who disciplines his son. it looks harsh, but the root is love. if you correct, he says, correct out of love.

original.note: Greek: love. The word in 1 John 4:7, the letter Augustine was preaching on.

trapdoor: what you thought: love, and do what you will means anything goes.
what it means: love is the root you check every act against. the act itself may be gentle or strict.
what a scholar hears: the line comes from Augustine's sermons on the first letter of John, in a passage about correcting others, not about license.

Hook says the line 'can be quoted like' a permission slip; no claim about how often. Confirm tone.
